source_text: Sic nec de aliquibus insignibus. Ceterum satis inhumanum, si feminae quidem per omnia viris subditae honorigeram notam virginitatis suae praeferant, qua suspiciantur et circumspiciantur et magnificentur a fratribus, viri autem tot virgines, tot spadones voluntarii, caeco bono suo incedant, nihil gestantes quod et ipsos faceret illustres. Debebunt enim et ipsi aliqua sibi insignia defendere, aut pennas Garamantum, aut stropulos barbarorum, aut cicadas Atheniensium, aut cirros Germanorum, aut stigmata Britonum: aut ex diverso fiat, capite velati in ecclesia lateant. Certi sumus spiritum sanctum magis masculis tale aliquid subscribere potuisse, si feminis subscripsisset, cum praeter sexus auctoritatem etiam ipsius continentiae nomine masculos potius honorari oportuisset. Quorum quanto sexus avidior et caldior in feminas, tanto continentia maioris laboratior ideoque dignior omni ostentatione, si ostentatio virginitatis est dignitas. Non enim et continentia virginitati antistat, sive viduorum, sive qui ex consensu contumeliam communem iam recusaverunt? Nam virginitas gratia constat, continentia vero virtute. Non concupiscendi cui concupiscendo inoleveris grande certamen est. Cuius autem concupiscendi ignoraveris fructum, facile non concupisces, adversarium non habens, concupiscentiam fructus. Quomodo ergo non magis viris aliquid tale deus in honorem subscripsisset. vel quia familiariori scilicet imagini suae, vel quia plus laboranti? Si autem nihil masculo, multo magis feminae.
thought_title: No insignia for virgins if men lack them
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that virgins deserve no special marks of honor, since men who practice continence receive none.
pass_a_gloss: So not from any insignia either. But it is quite inhuman, if women indeed, subjected to men in all things, carry before them the honor-bearing mark of their virginity, by which they are looked up to and looked around at and magnified by the brothers, but men, so many virgins, so many voluntary eunuchs, walk about with their own good hidden, carrying nothing which would also make them distinguished. For they too ought to claim some insignia for themselves, either the feathers of the Garamantes, or the headbands of the barbarians, or the cicadas of the Athenians, or the hair-knots of the Germans, or the tattoos of the Britons: or let it be done from the opposite, let them lie hidden in the church with veiled head. We are certain that the Holy Spirit could have prescribed something of this kind more for males, if he had prescribed it for females, since beyond the authority of sex, even by the very name of continence, males ought rather to have been honored. Of whom the sex is so much more eager and hot toward women, so much is their continence of greater labor and therefore more worthy of all display, if display of virginity is a dignity. For does not continence also surpass virginity, whether of widowers, or of those who by consent have now refused the common insult? For virginity consists of grace, but continence of virtue. Not to desire, when you have grown accustomed to desiring, is a great contest. But of that of which you have not known the fruit of desiring, you will easily not desire, not having an adversary, the desire of the fruit. How then would God not rather have prescribed something of this kind for men in honor, either because to his more familiar image, or because to the one laboring more? But if nothing for the male, much more nothing for the female.

choices.english: the honor-bearing mark of their virginity
choices.why: Keeps the compound adjective literal and preserves the idea that the mark itself carries honor.
rejected: the honorable badge of their virginity
the mark of honor of their virginity

choices.why: Caecus literally means blind; applied to the good, it means unseen or hidden, which fits the contrast with public display.
Stropulus is a rare word for a twisted band or fillet worn on the head; headband is the clearest literal rendering.
The cicada was a golden ornament worn in the hair by Athenians; keeping the literal insect name preserves the cultural reference.
rejected: the golden grasshoppers of the Athenians

choices.why: Stigma literally means a mark or brand; tattoos is the standard rendering for body marks of the Britons.
rejected: the painted marks of the Britons

choices.why: Contumelia means insult or outrage; communem means shared or common, referring to sexual intercourse as a shared degradation.

pass_b_english: So it is not with any other marks of distinction. It would be quite inhuman if women, who are subjected to men in everything, were to display the honor-bearing mark of their virginity, by which they are looked up to, noticed, and praised by the brothers, while men—so many virgins, so many voluntary eunuchs—walk about with their own good hidden, carrying nothing that would make them distinguished too. For they would have to claim some insignia for themselves as well: the feathers of the Garamantes, the headbands of the barbarians, the cicadas of the Athenians, the hair-knots of the Germans, or the tattoos of the Britons. Or let the opposite happen: let them hide in church with veiled heads.

We are certain that the Holy Spirit could more readily have prescribed something like this for males, if He had prescribed it for females, since apart from the authority of sex, males ought rather to be honored in the very name of continence. The more eager and hot their sex is toward women, the greater and more laborious their continence is, and therefore the more worthy of every display—if display of virginity is a dignity. Does not continence rank above virginity, whether that of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have already refused the common insult? For virginity consists of grace, but continence of virtue. It is a great struggle not to desire what you have grown accustomed to desiring. But when you have never known the fruit of desire, you will easily not desire it, since you have no adversary—the desire for the fruit. How then would God not more readily have prescribed something like this for men in their honor, either because they are closer to His own image, or because they labor more? But if nothing was prescribed for the male, much less for the female.

problems.quote: So it is with any other marks of distinction.
problems.why: Latin includes negation “nec” (nor), indicating a negative statement; English omits it, changing the meaning.
problems.fix: Thus, it is not concerning any insignia.
problems.ruling: Latin 'nec' = 'nor/not'; English 'So it is with' omits negation, changing meaning.

problems.quote: Does not continence surpass virginity, whether that of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have already refused the common insult?
problems.source_quote: Non enim et continentia virginitati antistat, sive viduorum, sive qui ex consensu contumeliam communem iam recusaverunt?
problems.why: Latin says continence does not stand opposite virginity (i.e., is not contrary), not that it surpasses it; English adds “surpass” and changes the relationship.
problems.fix: Indeed, continence does not stand opposite virginity, whether of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have already refused the common insult.
problems.ruling: 'antistat' = stands opposite/against, not 'surpass'; mistranslates the relationship between continence and virginity.

edits.old: So it is with any other marks of distinction.
edits.new: So it is not with any other marks of distinction.

edits.old: Does not continence surpass virginity, whether that of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have already refused the common insult?
edits.new: Does not continence stand opposed to virginity, whether that of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have already refused the common insult?

fixed: Added negation to match 'Sic nec de aliquibus insignibus'.
Changed 'surpass' to 'stand opposed to' to match 'virginitati antistat' (stand opposite/opposed), not surpass.

problems.quote: Does not continence stand opposed to virginity
problems.source_quote: Non enim et continentia virginitati antistat
problems.why: antistat means 'stands before, surpasses'. The argument is that continence outranks virginity. 'Stand opposed to' reverses that claim and breaks the logic of the next sentences.
problems.fix: Does not continence rank above virginity, whether that of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have already refused the common insult?

edits.old: Does not continence stand opposed to virginity
edits.new: Does not continence rank above virginity

fixed: Fixed `stand opposed to` -> `rank above`: source `virginitati antistat` means surpasses/stands before, not opposes; continence outranks virginity per following grace/virtue contrast.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker as Tertullian throughout, made pronoun references explicit (God, the Holy Spirit, men, women), and adjusted sentence rhythm for natural modern reading while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: the feathers of the Garamantes, the headbands of the barbarians, the cicadas of the Athenians, the hair-knots of the Germans, or the tattoos of the Britons
notes.why: These peoples and their customs are unexplained; reader cannot place them.
notes.fix: Briefly note these are exotic peoples whose distinctive adornments Tertullian lists as parallels.

last_rejected.quote: It is a great struggle not to desire what you have grown accustomed to desiring.
last_rejected.source_quote: Non concupiscendi cui concupiscendo inoleveris grande certamen est.
last_rejected.why: Source says it is a great struggle NOT to desire what you have grown TO desire; English reverses the sense.
last_rejected.fix: Not to desire what you have grown to desire by desiring is a great struggle.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin says "non concupiscendi...inoleveris" = struggle not to desire what one is accustomed to desiring; English matches.

last_rejected.quote: since you have no adversary—the desire for the fruit.
last_rejected.why: Source means 'not having desire as an adversary'; English makes 'desire for the fruit' the adversary you lack, garbling the sense.
last_rejected.fix: not having desire as your adversary, the desire for the fruit.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin "adversarium non habens, concupiscentiam fructus" = having no adversary, i.e., desire for fruit; English reflects this.

last_rejected.quote: because they are closer to His own image
last_rejected.source_quote: vel quia familiariori scilicet imagini suae
last_rejected.why: Men are themselves God's nearer image; the English makes the image something they approach.
last_rejected.fix: either because they are the more intimate image of Himself, or because they labor more
last_rejected.ruling: "familiariori ... imagini suae" = more familiar/closer to His image; "closer to His own image" is within range, and the image remains God's, so the sense is preserved.
